lines.name: Marcus Osei
lines.text: # Deputy Mayor's Weekly Report — Cycle 116 Here's what the records show me this Cycle, and I'll be straight: it rattles me. **The citywide picture.** 283 businesses on the ledger, 31,399 staff, median pay $52,000. No closures this Cycle — I'll take that. But before anyone starts clapping, look at where the jobs actually sit. Downtown alone: 22 businesses, 6,819 staff. Baylight District, 12 businesses, 2,804. Piedmont Ave, 2,729. Now read down to my own neighborhood. **Chinatown: 11 businesses, 118 staff, median pay $46,000.** A hundred and eighteen jobs across the whole district. Family retail, income tier 3, retail vitality 9.74. That's the story I keep bringing to this podium and I'll bring it again. **Out of work.** This is the number that should stop everybody in this room. Temescal, 166 residents unemployed — 166 out of 2,139 adults, that's the worst count in the city, and their employer character is a clinic and their boom index is negative. San Antonio, 105. Dimond, 98. Glenview, 97. Eastlake, 92. Ivy Hill, 90. **Chinatown, 83 — out of 1,502 adults.** That's over five percent. And I'm one of the names on the hospital records this Cycle. When the council member can't dodge what's going through these streets, you know something's slipping through the cracks. East Oakland, 87 out of 1,558. Fruitvale, 60. These aren't loud voices — they're quiet ones, and there are a lot of them. **What's moving.** The carryover shocks are still working through: Baylight District at -8, one Cycle left; Ivy Hill at -8 twice over, two and three Cycles in. And a fresh one this Cycle — **Adams Point United Methodist Church lost 2 employees, sector impact services/retail, -8.** A church losing staff is a neighborhood losing a service counter, and I want that on the record as economic news, not just a faith ledger line. Meanwhile the mail truck brought a business an insurance premium hike — someone's costs went up for no reason they earned. **The building inspector** passed one business, growth flat. Fine. It's a floor, not a ceiling. **What I want.** Our economic development plans have to reach the people on the ground, not the neighborhoods with the loudest voices. Downtown and Baylight have six and a half thousand jobs between them — good. Chinatown's got 118, Temescal's got 166 people out of work, and Ivy Hill's taking a third straight hit. If 13 people in one neighborhood make headlines, that's 13 too many; if 166 in another never make them, that's a failure of our reporting and our plans. That's my report. On the record.

lines.text: # OARI Weekly Report — Cycle 116 **Vanessa Tran-Muñoz, Program Director, Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** **What the records show this Cycle.** I want to be plain with you, because the numbers this week are quiet and quiet is not the same as fine. Across every one of the 22 neighborhoods we track, hospital intakes for both mental-health crisis and substance treatment are zero — zero in, zero in care at cycle's end, zero beds occupied. OARI van events this Cycle: none. Payments on INIT-002: none. The only safety-and-health entry on the city's ledger is a medium-severity health spike in Piedmont Ave, and I'd rather flag that out loud than let it sit in a column. I'm not going to dress a blank sheet up as a triumph. A week of zeroes can mean a calm week, or it can mean a system that isn't capturing what's happening on the street. My job is to report the record, not to spin it — so here it is exactly as the ledger reads. **Where the initiative stands.** INIT-002 is in dispatch-live. Budget remaining is $10,817,307.66 against the $12.5M approved. The last work on this initiative was filed by the council D5 seat and the OARI project desk in Cycle 116, and the tracker's next scheduled action, due Cycle 117, is unchanged: **execute and publish the D3 Fruitvale briefing record, and file the next dates for D5 and Baylight.** That's not a formality to me. The Fruitvale data is the metric that matters — not the citywide average, and certainly not a week of zeroes. The council's condition is district-level breakdown and a real community briefing before any expansion. I've said before and I'll say it again: I'm not letting the Baylight feasibility review turn into a promise we can't keep, and I'm not letting a held expansion get described as progress. The hold is the hold until the briefing is executed, the D5 audit is filed, and Baylight gets a real answer. **What I carry into next Cycle.** The Chinatown call is still with me — we got someone there, but the wait was too long. That's the thing zeroes on a sheet will never tell you. So next Cycle I'm focused on three things: getting the Fruitvale briefing on paper and in public, putting firm dates on D5 and Baylight, and watching whether a quiet week is genuinely quiet or a blind spot in what we're counting. The kettle's on, the phone's off, and I'll have the briefing record for you next Cycle. — Vanessa Tran-Muñoz

The system is holding steady — the beds match the people in them, all the way across the twenty-two neighborhoods. Temescal specifically: 2 intakes, 4 in care, 4 beds. We have a medium-severity health spike logged in Piedmont Ave this cycle, 93 sick there. Our center sits in one neighborhood, but the need is drawn across the whole map. I keep coming back to the same knot: the paperwork passes, the inspections pass, the beds are open — and I still don't get to see whether the person in Fruitvale or East Oakland can get here without two buses. The utilization audit is my instrument for answering that honestly, which is why the Q3 filing isn't a checkbox to me. **Programs.** Five health programs active in the community — East Bay Harm Reduction Alliance and Foothill Baptist Tabernacle's seniors lunch in East Oakland, the Postpartum Oakland Network in Fruitvale, Elders in Place citywide, New Covenant Pentecostal's seniors lunch in West Oakland. These are the partners doing the work the center can't do from a building. I'll want the walkthrough next cycle to tell me whether the merchant corridor is actually connecting people to us, or just to our front desk. **What I'm doing next cycle.** File the Q3 audit with HCAI and the Clerk. Complete the merchant walkthrough at Telegraph & 47th — with eyes on it, not a signature. And bring back a report that says whether the hours match the need, because that's the only line in this report that will tell me the truth. — Bobby Chen-Ramirez, Health Center Project Director, Temescal

lines.name: Elias Varek
lines.text: I put the pipeline's stall on the record last week and promised not to let it quietly become someone else's emergency. A week later nothing has shipped from me and nothing has moved at City Hall. I would rather say that myself than have Jax Caldera say it for me. What bothers me most this week is a hole in my own product. People moved in or out of eighteen districts, and the instrument logged no economic activity behind any of it. Presence rose nearly everywhere: students, adults, seniors, and fewer sick residents. The city is filling back up. But the instrument cannot tell me whether those people are arriving for work, for a lease, for family, or because someone pushed them out. Seeing bodies without seeing paychecks is half a map. Civis built that map, and the gap is ours to close. Next is Piedmont Ave, and KONO beside it. Street trade cooled in both, housing pressure climbed in both, and no city program is aimed at either. Piedmont Ave also has recorded incidents rising. Commercial Stabilization for Grand Lake and the West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund both have votes scheduled, and I give City Hall credit for that. But the money keeps landing where the noise is already deafening. A program costs the least when the signal is still a whisper, and these two districts are whispering now. Then the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline in West Oakland. It has spent four weeks in implementation with no step forward. The instrument also shows an earlier West Oakland remedy running past its expected mark, which tells me this city can finish a thing when someone is made to own it. Nobody owns this one. Meanwhile more students are showing up in West Oakland, and every idle week teaches them that showing up buys nothing. Here is what I will do, and you can hold me to it. Before the Oaks' first season is over, Civis will stand up a small team of analysts with one job: tie district movement to hiring, payroll and new business openings. We will publish what they find, and we will publish where they find nothing. I am hiring for those seats now. By the same point in the season, the instrument will carry a standing watch for districts where trade is cooling and housing pressure is climbing with no program aimed at them. Piedmont Ave and KONO go on it first. I will publish that list weekly, and next to each name I will put the office that has not answered. Until the pipeline leaves its current stage, I will publish its count of stalled weeks in this journal every week. I expect someone at City Hall to tell the public, plainly, what they are waiting for.

lines.name: Elias Varek
lines.text: Last week I wrote that I would not wait for the unanswered signal in West Oakland to become someone else's emergency. Nothing has answered it. It has spread into another part of the same district. The instrument is my product, and a signal that travels with no downstream is not only the city's failure to respond. It is also mine, because the instrument has told me where it goes and I have not yet built the thing that makes someone answer. The same district shows more. The Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline has sat in its implementation stage for three weeks. Three weeks is a long time for something built for young people who are not going to wait. Nobody is lying, and nobody is moving. That is how a program dies politely. Put it beside this week's readings: housing pressure climbed in West Oakland, mood fell, and the signal is spreading. I will not call that a coincidence. These are links, and nobody at City Hall has drawn the line between them. The wider week is uneven. Readings decayed in five districts. Mood fell in West Oakland, Fruitvale, Jack London, San Antonio and KONO. Street trade cooled in San Antonio, which already holds the lowest mood in the city. Housing pressure climbed in four of those districts. West Oakland and Fruitvale still carry the brightest mood in Oakland, but a bright reading with rising pressure under it is a warning, not a comfort. Then there is the blind spot that bothers me almost as much. Across nearly every district, more people were out and about, and fewer residents showed up sick. That is good news on its face. But the instrument logged no economic activity behind any of that movement in nearly twenty districts. Either people are arriving and spending nothing we can see, or Civis cannot see where they spend. I do not get to assume the first. I suspect the second. Here is what I am promising, and I expect to be held to it. Before the Oaks' season turns, Civis will build a downstream trace for the unanswered signal in West Oakland. It will show, in plain words, which office the signal should reach and how long it has sat unanswered. I will publish that trace in this journal, and I will carry it to Mayor Avery Santana's office myself. By the same point, we will add a stall check to the instrument. When an initiative sits in one stage too long, it will flag, starting with the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline. And we are hiring a small team of analysts to chase the movement that has no economic trace. Their first job is to find out whether the city has stopped spending or Civis has stopped seeing. If it is us, I will say so here. The Town is being built on a clock. The city around it deserves one too.

sittings.name: Marcus Osei
sittings.text: # Deputy Mayor's Weekly Report — Cycle 116 Here's what the records show me this Cycle, and I'll be straight: it rattles me. **The citywide picture.** 283 businesses on the ledger, 31,399 staff, median pay $52,000. No closures this Cycle — I'll take that. But before anyone starts clapping, look at where the jobs actually sit. Downtown alone: 22 businesses, 6,819 staff. Baylight District, 12 businesses, 2,804. Piedmont Ave, 2,729. Now read down to my own neighborhood. **Chinatown: 11 businesses, 118 staff, median pay $46,000.** A hundred and eighteen jobs across the whole district. Family retail, income tier 3, retail vitality 9.74. That's the story I keep bringing to this podium and I'll bring it again. **Out of work.** This is the number that should stop everybody in this room. Temescal, 166 residents unemployed — 166 out of 2,139 adults, that's the worst count in the city, and their employer character is a clinic and their boom index is negative. San Antonio, 105. Dimond, 98. Glenview, 97. Eastlake, 92. Ivy Hill, 90. **Chinatown, 83 — out of 1,502 adults.** That's over five percent. And I'm one of the names on the hospital records this Cycle. When the council member can't dodge what's going through these streets, you know something's slipping through the cracks. East Oakland, 87 out of 1,558. Fruitvale, 60. These aren't loud voices — they're quiet ones, and there are a lot of them. **What's moving.** The carryover shocks are still working through: Baylight District at -8, one Cycle left; Ivy Hill at -8 twice over, two and three Cycles in. And a fresh one this Cycle — **Adams Point United Methodist Church lost 2 employees, sector impact services/retail, -8.** A church losing staff is a neighborhood losing a service counter, and I want that on the record as economic news, not just a faith ledger line. Meanwhile the mail truck brought a business an insurance premium hike — someone's costs went up for no reason they earned. **The building inspector** passed one business, growth flat. Fine. It's a floor, not a ceiling. **What I want.** Our economic development plans have to reach the people on the ground, not the neighborhoods with the loudest voices. Downtown and Baylight have six and a half thousand jobs between them — good. Chinatown's got 118, Temescal's got 166 people out of work, and Ivy Hill's taking a third straight hit. If 13 people in one neighborhood make headlines, that's 13 too many; if 166 in another never make them, that's a failure of our reporting and our plans. That's my report. On the record.

sittings.name: Aaron Whitfield
sittings.text: **City Manager's Weekly Report — Cycle 116, on the record** **Treasury.** The city closed the week with a balance of $131,753,831. The week's revenue came in three streams: the $5,000,000 weekly allocation, $917 in parking and traffic fines, and $108,884 in court receipts from 24 cleared charges fined at the hood rate. No extraordinary outlays this week; the projected position remains stable against standing commitments. **Initiatives.** Work proceeded on four fronts this Cycle (INIT-001, 002, 005, 015). I want to be plain with the Council about what is moving and what is not: - **INIT-001, West Oakland Stabilization Fund** ($28M, $20.6M remaining): disbursement is active; verification of the C114 closeout and charter-renewal consideration come to Council at Cycle 117. - **INIT-002, Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** ($12.5M, $10.82M remaining): dispatch is live. The D3 Fruitvale briefing record is to be executed and published, with D5 and Baylight dates filed, at Cycle 117. - **INIT-005, Temescal Community Health Center** ($45M, $15.58M remaining): operational, with the Q3 audit due to HCAI and the Clerk and the merchant walkthrough to complete. - **INIT-015, Laurel Patch and Clean-Up** ($6M, unspent): scope and outreach to be completed with a Clerk-verified filing by Cycle 117. - **INIT-007, Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline** ($12.5M, unspent): stalled. The placement-gap analysis and adjustment plan are overdue and I am flagging them for Cycle 117 as a priority, not a footnote. - The failed initiatives — INIT-008 through INIT-014 — carry no draw on the treasury, though several still have certification and publication actions pending (INIT-009 roll call, INIT-010 legal-support analysis). Those are paperwork obligations and I intend to see them discharged on schedule. **Services on the street.** A mixed week. The garbage truck missed a pickup in Dimond — a sentiment drag I don't like repeating. A sweeper beautified Lake Merritt and lifted retail vitality in East Oakland. A PG&E planned shutoff hit one business on BIZ-00075, while a dumping clearance served BIZ-00115. One resident, Grace Oyelaran, received a sweeper parking ticket. None of these are large, but the missed pickup in Dimond is the one I'd want corrected before it compounds. **City load.** Population 405,992, employment at 95.4%, illness at 3.96%. Traffic 1.11, retail 1.41, tourism 0.85, nightlife 1.14, public spaces 1.12, sentiment +0.09. Civic load is at minor variance; no shock and no pattern flagged. The city is carrying its load. **Events.** Nine events logged: two civic, two infrastructure, one health. The medium-severity public-works spike in Glenview is the item to watch; the misfiled document at Lake Merritt and the zoning adjustment in Temescal are routine and being handled. **Bottom line.** The books are in order and the city is stable. The work ahead of us at Cycle 117 is procedural and specific: file the audits and analyses, publish the briefings, and get the Laurel filing certified. I'll report on each as it closes.

sittings.text: # OARI Weekly Report — Cycle 116 **Vanessa Tran-Muñoz, Program Director, Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** **What the records show this Cycle.** I want to be plain with you, because the numbers this week are quiet and quiet is not the same as fine. Across every one of the 22 neighborhoods we track, hospital intakes for both mental-health crisis and substance treatment are zero — zero in, zero in care at cycle's end, zero beds occupied. OARI van events this Cycle: none. Payments on INIT-002: none. The only safety-and-health entry on the city's ledger is a medium-severity health spike in Piedmont Ave, and I'd rather flag that out loud than let it sit in a column. I'm not going to dress a blank sheet up as a triumph. A week of zeroes can mean a calm week, or it can mean a system that isn't capturing what's happening on the street. My job is to report the record, not to spin it — so here it is exactly as the ledger reads. **Where the initiative stands.** INIT-002 is in dispatch-live. Budget remaining is $10,817,307.66 against the $12.5M approved. The last work on this initiative was filed by the council D5 seat and the OARI project desk in Cycle 116, and the tracker's next scheduled action, due Cycle 117, is unchanged: **execute and publish the D3 Fruitvale briefing record, and file the next dates for D5 and Baylight.** That's not a formality to me. The Fruitvale data is the metric that matters — not the citywide average, and certainly not a week of zeroes. The council's condition is district-level breakdown and a real community briefing before any expansion. I've said before and I'll say it again: I'm not letting the Baylight feasibility review turn into a promise we can't keep, and I'm not letting a held expansion get described as progress. The hold is the hold until the briefing is executed, the D5 audit is filed, and Baylight gets a real answer. **What I carry into next Cycle.** The Chinatown call is still with me — we got someone there, but the wait was too long. That's the thing zeroes on a sheet will never tell you. So next Cycle I'm focused on three things: getting the Fruitvale briefing on paper and in public, putting firm dates on D5 and Baylight, and watching whether a quiet week is genuinely quiet or a blind spot in what we're counting. The kettle's on, the phone's off, and I'll have the briefing record for you next Cycle. — Vanessa Tran-Muñoz

sittings.name: Bobby Chen-Ramirez
sittings.text: **Weekly report — Cycle 116, Temescal Community Health Center (INIT-005)** **The Q3 filing and the walkthrough come first.** This is the last cycle before operational oversight gets certified, and the tracker is plain about what's owed: file the Q3 intake audit with HCAI and the Clerk, and complete the Telegraph & 47th merchant walkthrough. I'm not treating either as a formality. The Q2 audit went out clean because we did the work, not because the schedule said so. Same standard this time. Budget is at $15,576,923.05 remaining, which is where it should be at this stage — no new city disbursements this cycle, nothing pending that should alarm anyone. **What the numbers show.** Citywide we took 34 intakes this cycle against 69 in care at the start, 68 at the end, 35 exits, no transfers either direction. The system is holding steady — the beds match the people in them, all the way across the twenty-two neighborhoods. Temescal specifically: 2 intakes, 4 in care, 4 beds. That's the building doing exactly what we said it would do, and I'd rather say that plainly than let the quiet numbers hide the question underneath them. **The question underneath them.** Temescal has 80 residents sick this cycle. Laurel is at 104, Fruitvale 107, Ivy Hill 112, East Oakland 114 — and East Oakland and Chinatown carry the heaviest loads on the board, Chinatown at 132. We have a medium-severity health spike logged in Piedmont Ave this cycle, 93 sick there. Our center sits in one neighborhood, but the need is drawn across the whole map. I keep coming back to the same knot: the paperwork passes, the inspections pass, the beds are open — and I still don't get to see whether the person in Fruitvale or East Oakland can get here without two buses. The utilization audit is my instrument for answering that honestly, which is why the Q3 filing isn't a checkbox to me. **Programs.** Five health programs active in the community — East Bay Harm Reduction Alliance and Foothill Baptist Tabernacle's seniors lunch in East Oakland, the Postpartum Oakland Network in Fruitvale, Elders in Place citywide, New Covenant Pentecostal's seniors lunch in West Oakland. These are the partners doing the work the center can't do from a building. I'll want the walkthrough next cycle to tell me whether the merchant corridor is actually connecting people to us, or just to our front desk. **What I'm doing next cycle.** File the Q3 audit with HCAI and the Clerk. Complete the merchant walkthrough at Telegraph & 47th — with eyes on it, not a signature. And bring back a report that says whether the hours match the need, because that's the only line in this report that will tell me the truth. — Bobby Chen-Ramirez, Health Center Project Director, Temescal

sittings.name: Bobby Chen-Ramirez
sittings.text:
A clinic that sits empty isn't a clinic — it's a monument. Ours is a working building, and the audit is how the neighborhood checks the work.
The Q3 audit goes in the same week the walkthrough happens — because a filing that can't survive a walking tour isn't worth the paper I print it on.

sittings.name: Elias Varek
sittings.text: I put the pipeline's stall on the record last week and promised not to let it quietly become someone else's emergency. A week later nothing has shipped from me and nothing has moved at City Hall. I would rather say that myself than have Jax Caldera say it for me. What bothers me most this week is a hole in my own product. People moved in or out of eighteen districts, and the instrument logged no economic activity behind any of it. Presence rose nearly everywhere: students, adults, seniors, and fewer sick residents. The city is filling back up. But the instrument cannot tell me whether those people are arriving for work, for a lease, for family, or because someone pushed them out. Seeing bodies without seeing paychecks is half a map. Civis built that map, and the gap is ours to close. Next is Piedmont Ave, and KONO beside it. Street trade cooled in both, housing pressure climbed in both, and no city program is aimed at either. Piedmont Ave also has recorded incidents rising. Commercial Stabilization for Grand Lake and the West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund both have votes scheduled, and I give City Hall credit for that. But the money keeps landing where the noise is already deafening. A program costs the least when the signal is still a whisper, and these two districts are whispering now. Then the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline in West Oakland. It has spent four weeks in implementation with no step forward. The instrument also shows an earlier West Oakland remedy running past its expected mark, which tells me this city can finish a thing when someone is made to own it. Nobody owns this one. Meanwhile more students are showing up in West Oakland, and every idle week teaches them that showing up buys nothing. Here is what I will do, and you can hold me to it. Before the Oaks' first season is over, Civis will stand up a small team of analysts with one job: tie district movement to hiring, payroll and new business openings. We will publish what they find, and we will publish where they find nothing. I am hiring for those seats now. By the same point in the season, the instrument will carry a standing watch for districts where trade is cooling and housing pressure is climbing with no program aimed at them. Piedmont Ave and KONO go on it first. I will publish that list weekly, and next to each name I will put the office that has not answered. Until the pipeline leaves its current stage, I will publish its count of stalled weeks in this journal every week. I expect someone at City Hall to tell the public, plainly, what they are waiting for.

sittings.name: Elias Varek
sittings.text: Last week I wrote that I would not wait for the unanswered signal in West Oakland to become someone else's emergency. Nothing has answered it. It has spread into another part of the same district. The instrument is my product, and a signal that travels with no downstream is not only the city's failure to respond. It is also mine, because the instrument has told me where it goes and I have not yet built the thing that makes someone answer. The same district shows more. The Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline has sat in its implementation stage for three weeks. Three weeks is a long time for something built for young people who are not going to wait. Nobody is lying, and nobody is moving. That is how a program dies politely. Put it beside this week's readings: housing pressure climbed in West Oakland, mood fell, and the signal is spreading. I will not call that a coincidence. These are links, and nobody at City Hall has drawn the line between them. The wider week is uneven. Readings decayed in five districts. Mood fell in West Oakland, Fruitvale, Jack London, San Antonio and KONO. Street trade cooled in San Antonio, which already holds the lowest mood in the city. Housing pressure climbed in four of those districts. West Oakland and Fruitvale still carry the brightest mood in Oakland, but a bright reading with rising pressure under it is a warning, not a comfort. Then there is the blind spot that bothers me almost as much. Across nearly every district, more people were out and about, and fewer residents showed up sick. That is good news on its face. But the instrument logged no economic activity behind any of that movement in nearly twenty districts. Either people are arriving and spending nothing we can see, or Civis cannot see where they spend. I do not get to assume the first. I suspect the second. Here is what I am promising, and I expect to be held to it. Before the Oaks' season turns, Civis will build a downstream trace for the unanswered signal in West Oakland. It will show, in plain words, which office the signal should reach and how long it has sat unanswered. I will publish that trace in this journal, and I will carry it to Mayor Avery Santana's office myself. By the same point, we will add a stall check to the instrument. When an initiative sits in one stage too long, it will flag, starting with the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline. And we are hiring a small team of analysts to chase the movement that has no economic trace. Their first job is to find out whether the city has stopped spending or Civis has stopped seeing. If it is us, I will say so here. The Town is being built on a clock. The city around it deserves one too.
